summary: On Tuesday, incumbent Rep. Wesley Bell defeated former Rep. Cori Bush in the Democratic primary for Missouri 's 1st Congressional District, securing the party nomination in his reelection bid.
The United Democracy Project, a super PAC of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee , funded Bell's campaign with more than $3 million in 2026, after spending more than $8 million in 2024.
Bush criticized Bell's support for Israel amid the war in Gaza and the West Bank, vowing in her concession speech, "Let me say this: AIPAC, I'm coming to tear your kingdom down!"
Nearly 60% of Democrats believe the U.S. is too supportive of Israel, according to a July poll; eighty percent of Democratic-leaning voters view the country unfavorably, according to April data.

Both Bush and Bell emerged from Ferguson's 2014 Black Lives Matter protests following Michael Brown's shooting. While Bush became a grassroots leader, Bell pursued local office and adopted reform policies to win his primary victories.
title: Source Icon

Detectives subsequently searched Taele's Downey residence, discovering an illegally modified AR-platform rifle, body armor, and notebooks containing "concerning statements," according to the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department.

The investigation, involving the FBI's Joint Terrorism Task Force and the Secret Service, also uncovered a loaded pistol and hollow-point ammunition in Taele's vehicle at the golf course, authorities said.

While the president prepares for Tuesday's Republican Party fundraiser, California Governor Gavin Newsom criticized the visit, noting residents await wildfire relief aid despite submitting more than $1.5 billion in claims.

Democrats expressed skepticism, noting the fund 'can easily be revived with a new order' after confirmation, and the current order fails to stop the Justice Department from compensating allies through other established processes.

summary: Spokane County Sheriff’s deputies arrested 37-year-old Aaron F. Farinacci on first-degree arson charges in connection with the Old Trails Fire, the largest of three blazes burning around eastern Washington's second-largest city.
A citizen tip proved key to identifying the suspect, after a witness reported seeing a nervous-looking man bending near grass shortly before smoke emerged at the fire's origin point on August 1.

Farinacci was initially questioned and released on the day the fire started, but major crimes detectives later pieced together evidence, body-camera footage, and the fact that he was carrying waterproof matches and a butane lighter when first detained.
The combined Spokane-area wildfires have destroyed over 700 structures and forced approximately 67,000 residents to evacuate amid extreme fire weather conditions.

Farinacci, who has a prior felony conviction for manslaughter in Arizona, is held on a $1 million bond ahead of his preliminary court appearance, while authorities continue investigating the causes of the other regional blazes.
title: Authorities arrest arson suspect in connection with one of the devastating Spokane wildfires

summary: On Aug 3, the Michigan Department reported two deaths linked to cyclosporiasis, stating both individuals had underlying health conditions that "may have been impacted by cyclosporiasis and dehydration."

Cyclosporiasis is a seasonal diarrheal illness caused by a parasite that commonly causes "explosive diarrhea" and hides in the rough, irregular surfaces of fresh produce like leafy greens and berries.
The CDC reports an acceleration of United States food-related illnesses this year, though no single source has been identified as the parasite is increasingly found on domestically grown produce.
Dr. Steven Goldberg of HealthTrackRx recommends manually cleaning produce under forceful water, avoiding bleach; he notes "prewashed" produce does not require additional washing at home.
With the cyclosporiasis season lasting through Aug 31, consumers should refrigerate cut or cooked produce within two hours to minimize illness risks during the remainder of the active season.
title: Michigan reports two deaths in ongoing cyclosporiasis outbreak

summary: The Suffolk County Department reported three confirmed cases of tularemia, also known as "rabbit fever," on Long Island this year, prompting health officials to warn residents.
Tularemia is a bacterial infection spread by tick bites or contact with infected animals, causing high fever and extreme fatigue that doctors say is more severe than Lyme disease.
Earlier this year, nine-year-old John Detmer required multiple rounds of antibiotics after a tick bite on his head caused weeks of severe pain and fever.
Health officials urge residents to perform daily tick checks and clean bite wounds with rubbing alcohol, monitoring for rashes for the next 30 days.

Experts predict a difficult tick season following a mild winter in New York, while the Suffolk County Department notes that confirming the rare diagnosis requires laboratory testing that can take several weeks.
title: What Is ‘Rabbit Fever?’ Health Officials Report 3 Probable Cases in New York

The proposed arrangement would allow safe passage through the strait, with northern inbound and southern outbound shipping lanes controlled by Iran and Oman respectively, and no toll payments.

summary: On July 14, 2026, the U.S. House passed the Sunshine Protection Act with a 308-to-117 vote, aiming to make daylight saving time permanent nationwide.

Proponents including Florida Congressman Vern Buchanan and Scott Yates argue permanent daylight saving time boosts economic activity and safety, while critics recall the failed 1974 experiment that resulted in three student deaths in the first 12 days.

Sleep expert Karin Johnson warned the Senate Committee that permanent daylight saving time disrupts circadian rhythms and increases health risks including stroke and seasonal depression, though supporters cite studies showing reduced robbery rates.

Under the legislation, states can choose between permanent standard or daylight saving time, addressing geographic disparities; Florida previously signaled intent to adopt year-round daylight saving time in March 2018.

With clocks set to fall back on November 1, expectations for immediate federal action remain low as Senate Majority Leader John Thune remains uncommitted regarding the federal mandate, potentially leaving states to decide independently.
title: Trump backs House-passed bill to make daylight savings time permanent

summary: On Tuesday, Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee endorsed Charlie Hatcher in the Republican primary for Tennessee's 5th Congressional District, challenging incumbent Rep. Andy Ogles.

Lee said he has known Hatcher for 25 years through their farming and business backgrounds. Hatcher, a fifth-generation dairy farmer, served as Agriculture Commissioner for seven years in Lee's administration.

The Invest in Tomorrow Coalition has spent about $2 million on advertisements supporting Hatcher while criticizing Ogles' congressional record. The race pits the incumbent aligned with the House Freedom Caucus against a former cabinet official.
Voters head to the polls this Thursday to decide the primary contest. While Hatcher promises to support President Donald Trump's agenda, Trump has endorsed Ogles, who is seeking a third term.

The primary winner will advance to the November general election, where the GOP is favored to hold the seat. As of Monday, Decision Desk HQ gives the GOP a 95 percent chance against Democratic challenger Chaz Molder.

McKinney leveraged an endorsement from President Donald Trump and $982,000 in fundraising to outpace GOP rivals Jerrod Sessler and state Sen. Matt Boehnke in the crowded Republican field.

Advancing with 30.8% of the vote, Duresky campaigned on affordability issues, including raising the federal minimum wage and strengthening labor protections endorsed by the Washington State Labor Council.
Separately, 5th District Republican Rep. Michael Baumgartner led his primary with 48% of the vote, seeking to defend the seat he won in 2024 against remaining challengers.

summary: On Wednesday, the Seoul Metropolitan Police Agency raided Starbucks Korea's headquarters to investigate a marketing campaign that critics claimed insulted victims of South Korea's 1980 Gwangju pro-democracy uprising.

Launched in May, the controversial 'Tank Day' promotion offered tumbler discounts alongside the phrase 'Put it on the table with a sound of 'Tak!'' which evoked memories of military suppression of demonstrators.

Investigators are examining whether company officials intentionally planned the event to insult democracy movement members after a civic group filed a defamation complaint against Shinsegae Group Chairman Chung Yong-jin.
Starbucks Korea fired CEO Son Jung-hyun and Chairman Chung issued apologies, while the company closed its more than 2,000 stores nationwide for mandatory social-sensitivity training.
Consumer brands operating in South Korea face significant risks navigating the country's historically sensitive political landscape, as this corporate crisis demonstrates.
title: South Korea Police Search Starbucks Korea HQ Over Investigation, Media Report Says

summary: On Tuesday, Maryland lawmakers passed a bill during a special session to place a redistricting question on the November ballot, clearing the House 96-38 and Senate 32-13 before awaiting Governor Wes Moore's signature.

Maryland Democrats argued the legislative push acts as a defensive measure against Republican-led states implementing similar efforts ahead of the 2026 midterms, framing redistricting as necessary protection.

Del Mark Fisher criticized the measure as "rigging elections" rather than balancing the Constitution, while Del Chris Adams warned it leads to "apathy, voter rejection of the process, and that's dangerous."

An amendment introduced by Representative Tom Hutchinson proposed a ballot question on whether the nine Eastern Shore counties should secede from Maryland, reflecting deep regional frustration over representation.

The bill does not redraw lines immediately but establishes that "nothing in the Maryland Constitution provides applicable criteria for the boundaries of a congressional districting plan," granting lawmakers significant future redistricting leeway.
title: Maryland lawmakers ask voters to clear the way for a congressional map designed to boost Democrats

summary: On Tuesday, Republican Rep. John James won Michigan 's GOP primary, securing his spot in November's gubernatorial election against Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson.
Backed by President Donald Trump, James defeated Perry Johnson, a Michigan businessman who spent $30 million on his campaign after previously spending $26 million on a failed 2024 presidential bid.
Repealing the state's 2023 Clean Energy and Jobs Act would be his "first priority" if elected, James said. He emphasized economy, immigration, and military support as platform pillars.

The Cook Political Report rates the race a "toss up, Lean D," while Mitchell Research polling conducted July 28–29 shows Benson leading James 46–44 percent to replace term-limited Gov. Gretchen Whitmer.
If James defeats Benson, he would become Michigan's first Black governor. Supporters like Christina Barr believe James's ability to listen to voters positions him as the strongest candidate.
title: Trump-backed John James wins Michigan’s GOP primary for governor

summary: On Tuesday, Kansas voters rejected a GOP-backed constitutional amendment to replace the merit-based Supreme Court nomination system with direct statewide elections, according to the Associated Press.
For nearly 70 years, Kansas has used a merit-based system where a nine-member Supreme Court Nominating Commission screens applicants for the governor to appoint, with justices serving six-year terms.

Republican Kansas Attorney General Kris Kobach spearheaded the amendment, citing the 2019 abortion ruling, while Former Kansas Supreme Court Chief Justice Lawton Nuss warned elections could compromise judicial integrity by inviting donor influence.

Emily Wales, president and CEO of Planned Parenthood Great Plains Votes, said, "We believed Kansans four years ago when they voted overwhelmingly to protect abortion rights in the state constitution." Kansas National Education Association President Sherri Schwanz praised educators who mobilized to defend schools.

The result preserves the nearly 70-year-old merit-based selection framework, halting conservative attempts to reshape the Supreme Court's ideological direction through electoral pressure on judicial candidates.
title: Kansas voters reject GOP-backed measure to directly elect state Supreme Court justices

summary: On Tuesday, Dane County Circuit Judge Everett Mitchell ruled that Wisconsin 's paper-based absentee voting program discriminates against disabled voters, denying them equal opportunity to vote privately and independently.
Disability Rights Wisconsin and the League of Women Voters filed the lawsuit in 2024, arguing that the lack of electronic absentee options violated protections of the Americans with Disabilities Act.

The Republican-controlled Legislature is fighting the lawsuit, even though Wisconsin currently emails ballots to military and overseas voters; neither the plaintiffs nor the Wisconsin Elections Commission provided estimates on potential electronic ballot demand.
Mitchell declined to immediately order electronic voting, citing disputes over whether that remedy is reasonable and noting risks involved in instituting such a program; a hearing is set for Aug. 12.

Spokespeople for the Wisconsin Elections Commission and the Wisconsin Department of Justice did not immediately return messages seeking comment, leaving the case outcome uncertain as legal proceedings continue.
title: Wisconsin judge rules that paper absentee ballots violate rights of certain disabled people

summary: On Tuesday, Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson won the Michigan Democratic gubernatorial primary with about 85% of the vote, decisively defeating Genesee County Sheriff Chris Swanson as hundreds of thousands of ballots remained to be counted.

Benson, a Harvard Law School graduate and former dean of Wayne State University Law School, previously won statewide elections in 2022 and 2018, positioning her as the expected frontrunner in the primary race.

Garnering key endorsements from the United Auto Workers, Benson's campaign reserved $10 million in advertising for September and October to shape the general election narrative against a fractured Republican field.

State Sen. Mallory McMorrow, D-Royal Oak, framed the general election as a contrast to Republican infighting, saying, "We literally cannot afford a governor who works harder for Donald Trump than they do for Michiganders."

title: Jocelyn Benson wins Democratic nomination for governor in Michigan

summary: Burlington-Based Judge Heather Cooper ruled on Tuesday that abuse claimants may pursue nearly 70 parish assets, potentially worth up to $500 million, to fund settlements in the Vermont Roman Catholic Diocese reorganization case.

The Vermont Roman Catholic Diocese filed for Chapter 11 protection in fall 2024 after paying $34.5 million to settle 67 misconduct lawsuits over two decades, yet it still faces 119 additional claims dating back to 1950.

Attorneys for more than 100 claimants argue the church must access these assets; Brittany Michael, lawyer for the claimants committee, told the Bankruptcy Court that "guidance from the court regarding the actual legal status of the assets" is necessary to reach a resolution.

Steven Kinsella of the Minnesota firm Fredrikson & Byron expressed concern that continued litigation threatens survivor compensation funds, noting the diocese has already spent $2 million in legal bills over two years.
Cooper warned that unless settled, the case could face years of litigation ahead, costing millions in attorneys' fees that could otherwise compensate abuse survivors.
title: Judge allows clergy abuse claimants to sue for parish assets in Vermont Catholic bankruptcy case

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the case as a civil-liberties abuse, stressing "coerced" confessions and even "wrongfully relying" on old Israeli convictions to deport a Palestinian mosque leader, while right-leaning coverage de-emphasizes the immigration drama and pivots toward Hamas as a "terror group," using harsher terms like "bullies," "intimidated," and "exclusive" to foreground threat and misconduct.
The key dividing line is whether the story is about prosecutorial overreach or security risk; the center stays more procedural, adding the ICE arrest and legal-resident status.
All sides still converge on the core testimony about pressured confessions and decades-old convictions, reflecting deeper divides over immigration, Israel-Palestine, and state power.
summary: On Tuesday, Salah Sarsour, the leader of Wisconsin's largest mosque, appeared in a Chicago immigration court to fight a United States deportation effort based on past Israeli convictions.

The Department of Homeland Security claims Sarsour poses a foreign policy threat based on 1980s and 1990s convictions in Israel, while Sarsour alleges the government is targeting him for speaking out against Israel.

Attorney Patrick Taurel presented testimony from Jawad Boulos, Sarsour's former lawyer, who alleged Israeli authorities tortured and coerced him into a plea deal involving weapon possession, not terrorism.

Mohammad Sarsour previously testified his brother appeared gaunt and in pain during Israeli detention, consistent with human rights reports alleging Palestinian prisoners face mistreatment and wrongful detention.

Sarsour is among several individuals arrested and threatened with deportation after speaking out for Palestinians since the Israel-Hamas war began in October 2023, with his next hearing scheduled for Sept 14.
title: US efforts to deport Palestinian mosque leader rely on coerced confessions, witness testifies

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Hoskins as blocking democracy, stressing a “gerrymandered” or “GOP-drawn” map and casting his constitutional claim as a “remarkable” excuse that shuts down a Trump-backed referendum ; right-leaning coverage is cooler and more procedural, centering that he “rejects” or deems the petition “insufficient,” while keeping Trump’s backing and Republican-led approval in view.

The sharp dividing line is whether the fight is partisan manipulation or lawful certification, with the center uniquely adding deadline-driven legal uncertainty, the court’s inability to know which map is active, and even “mob rule” rhetoric.
Both sides agree it is headed for court.
summary: On Tuesday, Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins rejected a citizen petition seeking a referendum on the state's new GOP-drawn congressional map, asserting the effort is unconstitutional because redistricting cannot be subject to voter referendums.

Lawmakers approved the "Missouri First" map 11 months ago to bolster the party's House majority, prompting the group People Not Politicians to submit more than 300,000 signatures to force a public vote.

Primary elections are proceeding today under the new districts, yet voters could face a different congressional map in November if courts overturn Hoskins' decision, creating significant confusion for candidates and voters.

People Not Politicians Executive Director Richard von Glahn vowed to challenge the rejection in court, citing public data showing the group gathered sufficient valid signatures well above the roughly 111,000 required.

Secretary Hoskins suggested state lawmakers could redraw the congressional map again in 2027, highlighting the persistent legal volatility surrounding redistricting efforts in Missouri and the potential for recurring map changes.
title: Missouri Election Chief Rejects Bid to Hold Public Vote on Trump-Backed Congressional Districts

summary: On Tuesday, the Toronto International Film Festival unveiled its 2026 Centrepiece lineup, showcasing 54 feature films from 50 countries, including auteur-driven works from directors Daniel Oriahi, Marie Clements, David Bezmozgis, and Cody Lightning.

TIFF expanded its overall programming by adding 70 total features across Centrepiece, Wavelengths, and Classics programs, marking an unprecedented eight animated films and a 4K restoration of Ken Russell's controversial 1971 drama 'The Devils'.

Animated selections include director Louise Bagnall's debut 2D feature 'Julian' and director Sebastien Laudenbach's 'Viva Carmen', while the Classics sidebar features five 4K restorations by directors Lynne Stopkewich, John Abraham, Fei Mu, and Kon Ichikawa.

Director Avi Nesher's 'Our Loves', his 21st film, joins the Centrepiece section; producers recently secured co-production deals with FOX Entertainment Studios and Access Entertainment, which SIPUR CEO Emilio Schenker described as countering an unofficial international boycott.
The 51st edition of the Toronto International Film Festival runs September 10 to 20, 2026, with organizers set to announce additional programming this week, building momentum for the event.
title: Israeli film about October 7 selected for Toronto International Film Festival despite boycott

summary: On Wednesday, nine Indonesians filed a complaint against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu , alleging crimes against humanity and piracy related to their detention during a Gaza aid mission in May.
The activists were part of the Global Sumud Flotilla intercepted by Israeli security forces in Oct 2025, during which more than 400 volunteers were detained for periods of days.

Their submission includes testimony about abuses they claim to have suffered during detention; Israel's treatment sparked international outcry after video showed volunteers kneeling with hands tied behind their backs.

Indonesia's criminal code grants courts "universal jurisdiction" over crimes committed beyond the country's borders, lawyer Kafin Muhammad said, enabling the investigation request into Zionist Israel that he filed.

Other nations including France, Italy, and Australia have already opened judicial investigations into the flotilla interception, establishing a pattern of international legal accountability for the May detention.
title: Indonesians File Complaint Against Netanyahu for Gaza Flotilla Arrest 'Abuses'

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames the story as a moral indictment, stressing “destruction,” “restrictions,” and “squandering” to portray Canadian aid as wasted by Israeli actions, while right-leaning headlines shift toward a broader, cautionary lens with phrases like “truth behind,” “dangerous,” and “life-threatening mission,” emphasizing aid-system fragility, obstruction, and threats rather than direct blame.
The sharpest dividing lines are the Canada Well damage, the April deaths of UNICEF water drivers, and whether restrictions are the central cause or merely one factor.
Both sides agree Gaza’s water work is perilous, but they diverge over who is responsible and what that implies geopolitically.
summary: On Tuesday, Jonathan Veitch, head of UNICEF for the Palestinian territories, reported that Israeli water infrastructure restrictions are squandering Canadian aid, citing destruction of the Canada Well facility.

Israel restricts items like cement and generators as 'dual-use' materials to prevent Hamas from building weapons, forcing UNICEF to become the 'provider of last resort' for water and sanitation services across Gaza.

Veitch described dire conditions where families live in makeshift tents surrounded by waste, with nighttime temperatures seldom dropping below 25 C and "millions and millions of rats" infesting the area.
The Israeli Defense Forces stated last week it is assessing infrastructure damage with severity, while 2.1 million Gazans remain confined to 30 per cent of the territory facing critical shortages.

Canada "punches above its weight" in humanitarian assistance, Veitch said, noting private donations helped end a recent famine, though he warned peace remains elusive as thousands grow up without education.
title: UNICEF Official Says Gaza Water Restrictions Waste Canadian Aid

bias: Left-Leaning coverage casts the White House UFC event as a “spectacle” that simply “lost $30 million,” stressing waste and performance over payoff; right-leaning coverage softens that blow by calling it a “celebration,” invoking “Freedom 250,” and arguing the “exposure” and deals made it “worth it,” even while noting the hefty loss.

Center-Leaning coverage sits between them, highlighting the record 34 million viewers, the $30 million hit, and even the fighter’s “lewd comments,” while also allowing for possible media and partnership upside.
Across all three, the shared frame is a costly Trump-attended event tied to Independence-era symbolism, but the ideological divide is over whether that cost signals fiasco or strategic spectacle.
summary: TKO Group Holdings revealed that its "Freedom 250" event on the White House South Lawn resulted in a loss of about $30 million, despite becoming one of the most-watched mixed martial arts events ever.

Production costs for the 4,300-seat arena reached about $60 million, and while President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance attended, the company could not recover expenses through sponsorships alone.
Despite the financial shortfall, the event drew 8.2 million viewers in the United States and about 34 million worldwide, making it one of the most-watched mixed martial arts events in history.

Andrew Schleimer, TKO Group's chief financial officer, told investors on Monday that the event "meaningfully impacted" margins, though the company "partially offset" costs with sold-out global partnerships inventory.

The event was shown exclusively on Paramount+ under a $7.7bn, seven-year contract signed last year; TKO noted "absent Freedom 250, margins would have increased year-over-year" for Q2, which saw revenue rise 29%.
title: UFC Parent Company Lost $30M on White House Fight

bias: Left-Leaning coverage frames Jack Smith ’s appearance as a procedural act of oversight, emphasizing that he “agreed” to testify and noting DOJ approval, while right-leaning coverage turns the same event into a partisan clash, using loaded terms like “EXPLOSIVE,” “NEW fire,” “thwart,” and “foremost targets” to suggest scandal and Republican combat.
The sharpest dividing lines are Trump, the prosecution, and right-only references to “Operation Arctic Frost,” subpoenas, and self-incrimination risk.
Center coverage stays more restrained, highlighting months of probing and Smith’s prior House testimony.
Both sides still agree on the Sept. 22 hearing, reflecting deeper divides over accountability versus political persecution.
summary: Senate Judiciary Committee Chair Chuck Grassley invited former Special Counsel Jack Smith to testify on September 22 regarding the Arctic Frost investigation into President Trump.
Grassley's invitation stems from records showing Smith's team subpoenaed text messages from 44 members of Congress and phone logs from a dozen senators during the probe.
In a letter obtained by The Hill, Smith's attorneys confirmed he will testify once permitted by the Justice Department, standing by decisions made as Special Counsel.
Grassley claims the investigation was "deeply flawed" and "weaponized," citing subpoenas of private communications and financial records from hundreds of Republican entities and individuals.
Last month, Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, referred Smith to the Justice Department for a "possible false statement" investigation, though Smith's lawyers maintain he testified truthfully under oath.
title: Jack Smith invited to testify before Senate Judiciary Committee next month
